text: Lower the pull minimum from $5 to $4 store-wide; hold Panini Prizm at $5+ (it's the worst fee-margin performer, not the low-price "sweet spot" prior notes assumed); worth testing $3 specifically for Panini Select / Topps Chrome.
detail:
Nine-agent data panel (2026-08-11), triggered by two ~$3 sales that seemed to contradict the Aug 6 $5+ policy. Key findings, each independently verified against real data:

1. FEE MATH SAYS LOWER, LABOR MATH SAYS DON'T GO TOO LOW. Using resale_flips_agent.py's real fee constants, and correcting the model to match how JC's listings actually charge shipping (buyer pays $1.32 separately, confirmed against 305/368 real sold rows), the true accounting breakeven is only ~$1.12 -- a $3 sale nets ~$1.61-1.71, solidly profitable on fees alone. But real per-card time data (docs/big_blue_scanner/guide.html: ~5.5 min to list + pull/ship time, 6-11 min all-in) means a $3 sale's EFFECTIVE HOURLY return is only $2.67-4.90/hr -- below minimum wage. Labor time, not eBay fees, is the actual binding constraint. $4 clears minimum wage more comfortably across the realistic time-estimate range.

2. PRIZM IS NOT THE SWEET-SPOT BRAND A PRIOR NOTE CLAIMED. That "Prizm = 44% of sales" note is stale/wrong -- current data shows Prizm is 14.1% of sales (Panini Select is the largest at 22.0%). Worse: 42.3% of all Prizm sales fall below the fee breakeven (worst of any major set), so a low floor specifically hurts on Prizm. Select and Topps Chrome, by contrast, show a real gap between genuinely-profitable $2-5 sales and the current $5 cutoff -- these are the sets actually worth testing lower.

3. SLOT SCARCITY IS REAL. The store already runs 2,807 active listings (over the prior 2,600-cap reference point). Cheap cards sit unsold 2-6x longer than expensive ones (sub-$5 median 9.6 days vs $15+ median 1.6 days, estimated from real item-ID-timestamp correlation, R²=0.9999) and return roughly 1/20th to 1/1000th the revenue-per-listing-slot-day of pricier items. This argues against a big drop, not for one.

4. OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD IS NOT A REAL OBJECTION. The marginal listings a lower threshold adds (~14 at $4, ~40 at $3) are a rounding error against 2,807 active -- the pipeline's existing bottlenecks (repricing backlog, photo-audit rotation, store-wide red Cassini scores) are a pre-existing scale problem unrelated to the low-value tail.

5. RETURN RISK: genuinely inconclusive -- this repo has no historical return/feedback-by-price data at all (sold_history.json's feedback field has been empty across all 368 rows; returns_plan.json only tracks currently-open returns, none historically logged). Not a factor either way today, but worth starting to track.

6. DATA GAP WORTH FIXING: inventory.csv and linkage.db haven't seen new scan intake since ~June 10 -- the panel could not actually evaluate "cards from the last week or so of scans" as asked, because that data doesn't exist yet in this repo. The backlog numbers above describe an ~2-month-old unpulled pile, not this week's scans. Re-sync CollX/scan intake before the next threshold review.

Dissent: the fee-margin and buy-radar-symmetry analyses argued the accounting floor alone would support $2-3 broadly; the labor-time and velocity analyses argued that's the wrong lens for a labor- and slot-constrained store and land closer to $4-5. This recommendation weights the labor/slot arguments more heavily since they're the ones grounded in this store's real, current constraints (2,807 listings, real per-card time data) rather than fee math in isolation.
